title: Bengaluru Techie's Website Reunites Nepal Flood Victims' Families With Data
excerpt: ReuniteIndia.com consolidates scattered official records into a single searchable database of people missing in the Nepal floods, with QR-coded live case pages.
body:
• A Bengaluru techie identified as Mohammad has built ReuniteIndia.com, a single searchable platform consolidating missing-persons records from the Nepal flash floods.
  • Each case page carries a QR code linking to the person's live status, plus a hospital and police-station locator near the last-seen location and guidance for filing a police complaint.
  • The site verifies crowdsourced information against official government reports and normalizes inconsistent Devanagari transliterations across bulletins.
  • The floods, which struck the Nepal-Tibet border region on August 26, have killed more than 675 people, with 22 people from Telangana still untraced.

As families across India and the diaspora scramble for news of loved ones missing in Nepal's catastrophic flash floods, a Bengaluru techie has built a website that does what dozens of helplines, PDFs, and WhatsApp forwards cannot: put everything in one place. The platform, ReuniteIndia.com, gathers scattered official records — disaster bulletins, police notices, hospital lists — into a single, searchable database of missing persons.

"Having all the information on a single platform helps families who are stuck right now to gather information scattered across dozens of PDFs, helplines and social media posts," the site's creator, Mohammad, told The Hindu.

What distinguishes the site is that each person's record stays current. "Each page of the case contains a QR code linking to the person's current status, so someone scanning an old poster can still see the latest information," Mohammad explained. The site also includes a hospital and police-station locator near the last-seen location, along with instructions on what to do if a police complaint has not yet been lodged.

A disaster that stranded thousands of pilgrims

The flash floods struck the Nepal-Tibet border region on August 26, with initial reports suggesting the sudden deluge may have been triggered by an ice-rock avalanche in the Lhende River rather than rainfall alone. Syapru Besi and Timure — key transit and acclimatization points for Kailash-Manasarovar pilgrims — were among the areas severely affected. With roads, bridges, and communication routes washed away, traditional search and rescue operations have struggled.

The death toll has surpassed 675, according to News18. In India, the Telangana government has confirmed that 22 people from the state remain untraced. A helpline at Telangana Bhavan in New Delhi has received 80 to 100 calls since August 26; after scrutiny, 20 cases concerning 23 persons were identified for action, including 17 Telangana-origin NRIs, officials said.

Among the missing is K. Suhasini Reddy, a 44-year-old software engineer based in Australia with roots in Hyderabad's LB Nagar. She had returned to Hyderabad on August 19 with her younger son for a housewarming ceremony, then traveled to Kathmandu on August 23 to join a friend for a Kailash pilgrimage. Her family last spoke to her on the evening of August 25.

Verification in a fog of rumor

Beyond consolidation, the site acts as a verification tool when unverified rumors and outdated posts circulate on social media. "We verify crowdsourced information directly with official government reports before confirming statuses," Mohammad said. The task is harder than it sounds: individual names in official Nepal Police bulletins often appear in Devanagari script or informal transliteration rather than standard English spelling, meaning the same person can surface under two or three different spellings in different sources. The platform resolves those into one consistent, English-accessible record — critical for Indian families, most of whom cannot read the Nepali bulletins.

He is now working on adding an AI chatbot to the site's resource page to answer families' questions directly.

"Each page of the case contains a QR code linking to the person's current status, so someone scanning an old poster can still see the latest information."

— Mohammad, creator of ReuniteIndia.com

Diaspora angle

The missing are disproportionately pilgrims and NRI tourists — 17 of the 23 Telangana cases involve Telangana-origin non-resident Indians — which makes diaspora-focused tools like ReuniteIndia.com vital. For families in Australia, the Gulf, and the U.S. watching from afar, a single verified, English-language record cuts through the noise of rumor and outdated posts in ways no helpline operating in Indian hours can.

What's next

Nepal Police continue rescue and identification operations, with AI facial recognition now being deployed to identify victims whose remains are too damaged for quick DNA matching. For the families of the still-missing, the site offers something official channels have struggled to deliver: one page, kept current, with every fact verified against government records.
